questions.title: Whose noon shadow falls on the park at the winter solstice?
questions.why: The X3D has each building's height and north face; the record has the sun (25.9° at noon on 21 December at 40.7° N, so a shadow runs 2.06 m per metre of height). A planning board sees which towers darken the park in the one season people most want sun.

questions.title: Which buildings stand in the flood zone?
questions.why: GeoSPARQL names the zone and its WKT; the scene gives the drawn footprint. (This page reads positions from the X3D, because none of its engines runs GeoSPARQL's geof: functions; a spatial store such as GraphDB or Jena with GeoSPARQL would test the WKT directly.)

questions.title: Which buildings are within a 400 m walk of the new stop?
questions.why: Transit-oriented zoning starts from a radius. The record holds the policy (400 m), the scene holds the distances, and the answer is the set of lots that could be upzoned.

inference.title: Buildings inherit their district from their parcel
inference.why: The record puts a building in a parcel and the parcel in a district. sfWithin chains, so a rule puts each building in its district, and the height rule below can read the district's limit.

fault_text: Tower 5 is drawn 48 m tall in a 36 m district, and Building 2 is drawn 8 m east, overhanging its parcel.
